robots.grabcad_model_description:
Chassis:
Our robot's foundation is a 28x28 inch chassis, designed with an eye for achieving the best balance and maneuverability on the 2024 game's open field. It is outfitted with SDS MK4i swerve modules, featuring L2 gear ratios and powered by NEO motors. The chassis design includes strategically placed slots for easier wiring and a honeycomb pattern belly pan that helps with organizing electronic components while also lowering the center of gravity to improve stability.

Intake
The intake system is directly inspired by the "Cranberry Alarm" RI3D team's design but adapted to fit our robot's specific requirements. The intake plates are made from polycarbonate, cut with our CNC router, and reinforced with aluminum to strengthen the areas identified as potential weak points. A “REV Through Bore Encoder” on the pivot shaft of the intake ensures precise control, allowing for accurate handling of game pieces.

Elevator:
Our elevator system borrows its simplicity and efficiency from the "Thrifty Elevator" design. It is equipped with a gearbox that has a 40:1 reduction ratio, eliminating the need for a ratchet system while securely holding the robot suspended on a chain post-match. The design includes hooks with inward slots to ensure a secure and stable climb. The precise movement is controlled by a “REV Through Bore Encoder” on the gearbox's output shaft.

Shooter:
Through testing, we identified a top-bottom style shooter as the most reliable for both consistency and range. This shooter is driven by two NEO motors, with power transferred via belts. The shooter's pivot is powered by a NEO motor connected to a MAX Planetary gearbox for fast gear ratio changes(if necessary), allowing for swift adjustments in shooting angles. A “REV Through Bore Encoder” on the shooter's pivot shaft provides the necessary precision for adjusting angles based on the target's distance.

Materials and Manufacturing Techniques:
The robot's structure is mainly made from 6061 aluminum alloy profiles and 5052 and 6061 sheet plates, creating a frame that is both strong and light. All sheet plates are finished with a semi-matte black anodize for aesthetic appeal. The manufacturing process involves precision milling and water jet cutting, with sheet plate component thickness standardized at 4mm and 6mm.

This is team 5036 2019 Robot for the game Deep Space. All the CAD was completed in AutoCAD inventor; various prototypes were built and tested in the shop to assure we built the most effective mechanism for the game. 
The Drivetrain is a AM14U3 kit bot chassis with a cutout at the front to help the Cargo(13 inch circumference ball) go through with ease. 
This robot has a cargo intake which springs back and forth on a piston. The intake has mecanum wheels to guide the ball toward the center and in the center has compliant wheels to guide the ball toward the conveyor. The conveyor system carries the ball upwards using a system of pulleys and belts. The intake is powered by a 775 and the conveyor through dual 775's.

This is my robotics team's robot for the 2018 FIRST Power Up competition. 
(For specific details about the robot, click "Show more...") 

We utilize SolidWorks 2017 3D CAD as our primary computer aided design software for this robot. As a team, we each take an element on the robot to design using SolidWorks and combine them into an assembly to create our robot.

My role as Lead Design Engineer (Student) is to lead the design/CAD team in designing a robot that is optimized for the competition and feasible for manufacturing. I also spend the preseason teaching other students on the team how to use SolidWorks.

For more information about us:
https://team1991.com
https://www.youtube.com/channel/UCPo0HSI_RKmutuLvsCoKSAg/featured
https://www.instagram.com/frcteam1991/
https://github.com/FRC1991

**************************************************

General Information About the Robot:
Our robot is comprised of 3 main components: the drive train, the intake, the elevator. Most the components on the robot are made of 0.125" 6061 aluminum alloy that has been laser cut and bent in a hydraulic press brake. By using this method we were able to consolidate much of the parts and make everything as one single part so that all we needed to do was throw on the nuts and bolts. 

The Drive Train:
Our chassis is built from a modular swerve drive system. 
Each wheel module can turn and drive independently, giving us the ability to “pan” as well as make sharper turns and various other maneuvers that traditional tank drives cannot perform.
This allows us to position the bot faster and easier. The versatility of the swerve drive makes it great for both offensive and defensive plays.
The design for the modules are based off of the VexPro VersaSwerve. We redesigned it so that the modules are enclosed and that the motors are on-top/closer to the robot

The Intake:
Our intake utilizes a unique method of intake by “reach grabbing”. The system uses bungees and intake wheels. The system also flips upside down to extend the height that the robot can reach. The flipping motion is pulley driven. 
We combined the flipping motion with the climber so that both components could be run on a single motor. It does so via a tether (not shown), that wraps around the climber winch and runs to the bottom of the climbing hooks.
The intake has gone through many variations of the intake. In the end we solved our problems with the “reach grabbing” method and by cutting weight by making it out of plastic...

FRC, or FIRST Robotics Competition, is the competition for high school students (grades 9-12), focusing on a robotics challenge released every January and promoting community outreach and education. For more information on FIRST and FRC, visit www.firstinspires.org.

Just wanted to share a project I've been working on for the past month or so to prepare myself for the upcoming season.
I took elements from my favorite robots of 2016 and reverse engineered them using photos I could find, then re-designed them using methods my team can use(e.g. no welding, certain screw sizes and suppliers etc.).
From those re-designed mechanisms, I've designed a full robot, ready to play the 2016 game, FIRST Stronghold.
I've learned a lot from this project, and I feel it's gotten me to a level where I feel comfortable designing almost anything.

Mechanisms used:
-971 Shooter+Hanger
-254 Intake
-My own design of a 8X8 WCD
-Generic hot-swappable PC Trianlges for defenses

(This does not include any sensors, cameras, a belly pan, screws or electronics because these are very boring and technical stuff and I got bored midway through)
